lesson.title: Investigating Loyalty: The House Un-American Activities Committee
lesson.summary: Although often confused with Joseph McCarthy in popular memory, the House Un-American Activities Committee was a separate, older body whose investigations into Hollywood and government employees, especially the Hollywood Ten and Alger Hiss cases, helped fuel and legitimize the broader climate of McCarthyism.
lesson.body:
It is a common mix up, but worth getting right: the House Un-American Activities Committee, usually called HUAC, was not run by Joseph McCarthy and was not even in the same chamber of Congress. McCarthy was a senator, and his investigations ran through Senate committees; HUAC was a committee of the House of Representatives, created in 1938, initially to investigate both Nazi and communist subversion. By the postwar years, though, HUAC had focused almost entirely on hunting for communist influence, and its work ran alongside, and helped reinforce, the same atmosphere of suspicion that McCarthy later rode to national fame.

HUAC's most famous hearings targeted the American film industry in October 1947, investigating supposed communist influence in Hollywood. Ten witnesses, screenwriters and directors who became known as the Hollywood Ten, refused to answer the committee's questions about their political beliefs and associations, citing their First Amendment rights. The committee and Congress did not accept that defense; all ten were cited for contempt of Congress and served prison sentences, and the episode triggered a broader industry blacklist that kept hundreds of writers, actors, and directors suspected of leftist sympathies from finding work for years, often without any proof of wrongdoing at all.

HUAC's other landmark case involved Alger Hiss, a former State Department official accused by an ex-communist writer named Whittaker Chambers of having passed government documents to the Soviets in the 1930s. A young congressman on the committee named Richard Nixon pursued the case aggressively, and it made his national reputation. Hiss could not be tried for espionage because the statute of limitations had expired, but he was convicted of perjury in 1950 for lying about his contacts with Chambers. The case remains debated by historians in its details, but at the time it convinced many Americans that communist infiltration reached into the highest levels of government, adding fuel to the fear that McCarthy would soon exploit on an even larger scale. Together, HUAC's hearings and McCarthy's Senate investigations formed a two pronged assault on civil liberties, one rooted in the House, the other in the Senate, that defined the anti-communist hysteria of the era.
